g.text: Two method signatures do most of the architectural work
One makes fire-and-forget impossible to accidentally undo; the other makes a global connection registry impossible to reintroduce.
What one WebSocket server actually holds
class Connection:
userId
socket
friends: Set<UserId> # ~400, read ONCE at connect
friendPositions: Map<UserId, Position> # last known - even if FAR
lastSelfPos: Position
radius: meters # per-user, configurable
Positions are cached even for friends who are out of range, for two reasons: the departure check below needs the PREVIOUS
position to know a transition happened, and a client that stops receiving updates can still render a friend at their last
known place with an honest timestamp.
interface ConnectionRegistry # PER-SERVER, not global
add(userId, conn) -> Connection? # the displaced older session
localConnectionsInterestedIn(friendId) -> List<Connection>
remove(userId)
The method is localConnectionsInterestedIn, and the NAME IS DOING WORK: it can only
answer about clients on THIS server. Making the interface incapable of answering
globally means nobody can quietly reintroduce the 333,000-lookups/sec global
'who is connected where' registry that the whole channel design exists to avoid.
interface ChannelBus
publish(channel, msg) -> void # no Future, no ack
subscribe(channels, handler) -> Subscription
unsubscribe(channels) -> void
publish returns NOTHING and takes no callback, so the signature ENCODES the
fire-and-forget requirement. A caller cannot accidentally start awaiting
confirmation, and a future maintainer cannot add retry logic without changing the
interface and having that conversation first. At 13.3M pushes/sec a per-message
ack would be a larger system than the one it protects.
friendGraph.friendsOf is likewise commented connect-time-only: it is a database
read, and on a path that runs 333,000 times a second it would be a 400-row query
per update.
Connect: 400 friends, but not 400 requests
onConnect(socket):
userId = authenticate(socket)
displaced = registry.add(userId, socket)
if displaced: displaced.close(SUPERSEDED) # the reconnect race
friends = friendGraph.friendsOf(userId) # ~400; connect-time ONLY
byNode = groupBy(friends, f -> router.nodeFor(channel(f)))
for node, channels in byNode:
bus.subscribe(channels, conn.onFriendUpdate) # ONE req per NODE
positions = locationStore.getMany(friends) # ONE MGET, not 400 GETs
-> compute distances, send { type: 'init', friends: nearby }
400 friends
groupBy(nodeFor(channel))
~133 requests
A 3x reduction per connection - and fewer in
practice, since friends cluster. Fleet-wide that
turns 4 BILLION subscriptions into ~1.3 billion
requests, which is the difference between a mass
reconnect being slow and being an outage.
onDisconnect(conn):
for f in conn.friends:
if registry.localConnectionsInterestedIn(f).isEmpty():
bus.unsubscribe([channel(f)]) # ONLY if nobody local needs it
registry.remove(conn.userId)
The reference count matters. Two clients on the same server may share a friend, and
unsubscribing on the first disconnect would silently stop updates for the second.
With ~100,000 clients per server, shared friends are common rather than
exceptional - so this is a real bug, not a theoretical one, and it fails SILENTLY,
which is the worst kind.
The two hot paths - 333,000/sec in, 13.3M/sec out
onLocationUpdate(conn, msg): # 333,000/sec
pos = Position(msg.lat, msg.lng, msg.ts)
if not isPlausible(pos, conn.lastSelfPos): # teleport / spoofing
metrics.increment('location.implausible'); return
if conn.lastSelfPos and
haversine(pos, conn.lastSelfPos) < MIN_MOVE_M:
conn.lastSelfPos = pos # keep the TS fresh
return # publish NOTHING
conn.lastSelfPos = pos
locationStore.put(conn.userId, pos, ttl=600s) # TTL = presence
historySink.append(conn.userId, pos) # async, droppable
bus.publish(channel(conn.userId), encode(pos)) # ONE. No ack.
onFriendUpdate(friendId, pos): # 13.3M/sec
for conn in registry.localConnectionsInterestedIn(friendId):
prev = conn.friendPositions.get(friendId)
if prev and pos.ts <= prev.ts: continue # out of order
conn.friendPositions[friendId] = pos # cache ALWAYS
d = haversine(conn.lastSelfPos, pos)
if d > conn.radius:
if prev and
haversine(conn.lastSelfPos, prev) <= conn.radius:
conn.send({type: 'friend_left', user_id: friendId})
continue
conn.trySend({type: 'friend_location', ..., distance_m: d})
movement suppression comes FIRST, before anything expensive
a stationary user - at a desk, asleep - generates an update every 30 seconds that changes nobody's screen. Suppressing
sub-threshold movement saves on both the write AND the 40x fan-out, and it should be permanent, not an overload measure.
Note it still updates lastSelfPos, so the timestamp stays fresh and the client's 'updated 4s ago' does not drift.
ordering is resolved by TIMESTAMP at the receiver, not by the transport
fire-and-forget pub/sub gives no ordering guarantee, and buying one would mean ordered channels with sequence tracking.
Comparing pos.ts against the cached position achieves the same user-visible outcome in one line, for free.
the friend_left edge is easy to miss and very visible when missing
if a friend walks out of range, a naive 'continue' means the client never hears about it - so the friend stays FROZEN on
screen at their last in-range position, forever, looking present. The in-range to out-of-range TRANSITION has to be an
explicit message. This is the classic bug in any radius-filtered push feed.
Almost nothing here is a race - which is the real payoff of the requirements
needs no lock at all
publishing an update one PUBLISH to the user's own channel. No shared
structure is touched, and there is nothing to be
consistent ABOUT - a subscriber gets it or does not.
distance computation a pure function of two positions.
the location cache each key is written only by the ONE server holding
that user's connection, and SET is atomic. Readers
see old or new, both acceptable inside 30 seconds.
out-of-order updates resolved by timestamp, not by locking or sequencing.
needs coordination - a short list
ConnectionRegistry a concurrent map: network threads add and remove
connections while onFriendUpdate iterates. The
returned list is a SNAPSHOT and trySend on a closed
socket is a no-op, not an error.
per-connection state PIN each connection to one event-loop thread, so all
its state is single-threaded and needs no
synchronization. Same technique as the stock
exchange - for a far less demanding reason.
the channel hash ring read constantly, written rarely: a copy-on-write
reference swap, so readers never block or tear.
The general shape, as everywhere in this guide: cross-process races belong to a shared store, intra-process races belong to a
thread assignment. Here almost nothing is a race at all, because the data is IDEMPOTENT-BY-OVERWRITE and LOSSY-BY-DESIGN.
Self-correcting data barely needs concurrency control.
Error cases, and why each handling choice is deliberate
error
handling
why it is deliberate
implausible position
reject, count the metric
a 500 km jump in 30 s is GPS error or SPOOFING. Publishing it shows a friend teleporting -
and spoofing is a real privacy attack: claiming to be near you to see who is around.
slow client socket
DROP the message; never block
blocking would stall the shared onFriendUpdate loop and penalise every other client.
A queued stale position is worse than none.
pub/sub node unreachable
resubscribe on the new owner
retrying the PUBLISH is pointless - the next update in <= 30 s supersedes it.
cache write fails
log, continue, still publish
the publish is what friends see; a cache miss only affects the next client to call init.
Failing the whole update to protect a cache write would be backwards.
friendsOf fails on connect
fail the connection, retryable
with no friend list there is nobody to subscribe to, so a 'successful' connection would
silently show an empty screen. Better to fail loudly.
duplicate session for one user
close the older one (SUPERSEDED)
otherwise the user publishes twice per interval and receives duplicates.
historySink unavailable
drop silently, circuit-break
an analytics gap must never affect the live feature.
